Assumptions as we targeted our communication and focus on what to recommend/ask in the table below:
CAN NOT HELP: We can't really help people using a space in an illegal way, and are getting kicked out by the landlord because of it.

CAN HELP A LITTLE: Someone using a space in an illegal way, who wants to get legal, and got a violation from the City. Might be too hard and take a lot more time to help since it may take changes to zoning and / or it is tied to their lease.

CAN HELP THE MOST:  Someone using the space they have in a legal way, and need help doing so.  For example, they have a commercial space, using for Making, don't live in it, but had no idea that they had to follow certain fire codes and now are in trouble.

After a quick perusal of the original Problem Statements I found the following related to Risk Management in the area of safety and training:
It is difficult for each space to create material for the training and tracking of member safety instruction or certifications.
Members of a space require clear, consistent training and documentation on key areas such as safety training, operational guides/best practices for key equipment.
Spaces often face challenge to figure out what laws, ordinances, zoning rules, or other guidelines apply to them.
Housekeeping is an ongoing challenge for spaces as members’ projects are often not cleaned up while in process or at the completion, occupying space and tools that others could be using.
Many Makerspaces have limited resources or knowledge to dispose of wastes such as e-waste, hazardous chemicals, or biological, or other non-standard waste.

Capture of the highlights of a discussion in Slack on December 12th, 2016 with Jeffrey McGrew on the different codes:
National, Industry or International Code Standards come out every three years.
Building Code, Fire Code, Electrical Code, and those sorts of 'how it gets built' codes are all based upon International Codes.
These International Code Standards get adopted into the State Code, which then gets additional modifications from the county or city to be the ‘local code’.
Another complexity is Zoning / Planning Code.
“How It’s Built” can be generalized, but “What Can Go Where” can’t be generalized.

KIPP: "Breaking the doc down, items #2 and #3 are reflective of what I would perceive as a negligent attitude. I can't understand why "immediate needs" would be "what to do if the fire marshal comes", and not "how to identify and correct safety hazards in your space". Shouldn't that be the goal of space organizers? Also "long term" goals shouldn't be "let's be legal", but they should be zero injuries, zero risk, and zero tolerance for hazards. Because even safe spaces have accidents. I remember the anguish from my colleagues at Yale when one of their students was killed:
https://yalealumnimagazine.com/articles/3288-after-a-fatal-accident-new-safety-standards
Even after that, most maker spaces still don't take a strict attitude towards these kinds of hazards in addition to fire safety."
